argument: After witnessing old age, sickness, death, and an ascetic during his four sights, Siddhartha Gautama abandoned his life of royal luxury and, after years of failed asceticism, found a middle way between indulgence and extreme self-denial, achieving enlightenment under the fig tree at Bodh Gaya. His resulting teaching, the Four Noble Truths, holds that dissatisfaction is the default state of the mind, that it is caused by attachment, aversion, and ignorance rooted in the delusion of a separate self, that it can be ended by dissolving that delusion, and that the Eightfold Path of morality, meditation, and wisdom is the practical route to nirvana — a permanent extinguishing of desire achieved entirely through one's own effort, with no God to answer to and no salvation dependent on belief.
keyIdeas: The doctrine of impermanence (anicca) holds that nothing — including both pleasure and pain — lasts very long; all existence, including the self, is in constant flux.
The Middle Way rejects both a life of sensual indulgence and a life of extreme ascetic self-denial, both of which the Buddha personally tried and found did not produce lasting insight or happiness.
The First Noble Truth holds that dissatisfaction (dukkha) is the default state of mind — even when satisfaction is achieved, the mind normalizes to it and the feeling fades.

The Second Noble Truth identifies three mechanisms through which desire produces suffering: attachment (assuming a thing will bring permanent happiness), aversion (reacting to unmet expectations about how the world 'should' be), and ignorance (believing happiness is controlled by external things).

The Third Noble Truth grounds the end of suffering in 'no-self' (anatta): the desire driving suffering is rooted in the delusion of a separate, bounded self, and recognizing the self as impermanent and interconnected — without denying experience outright — undercuts that root desire.

terms.def: The doctrine that nothing, including pleasure, pain, and the self, lasts very long; all existence is in constant flux.
The First Noble Truth's claim that dissatisfaction is the default state of mind, since satisfaction fades as the mind normalizes to it.
The path between sensual indulgence and extreme ascetic self-denial that the Buddha found, after personally testing both extremes and finding neither produced lasting insight.
The doctrine that there is no separate, bounded, permanent self; the delusion of such a self is the root of the desire that drives suffering.
Literally 'blown out,' referring to the extinguishing of the flames of desire, aversion, and ignorance — not an afterlife or annihilation.

The Buddha's guidebook to nirvana, organized into three categories: morality (right speech, action, livelihood), meditation (right effort, mindfulness, concentration), and wisdom (right understanding, resolve).
